source.title: Improved Scaling Laws via Weak-to-Strong Generalization in Random Feature Ridge Regression
source.authors: Di-Yuan Wu; Le-Han Chen; Theodor Misiakiewicz; Marco Mondelli

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong training in a new setting: random feature ridge regression, with teacher and student performance compared through test-error scaling laws rather than the original neural-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper analyzes and simulates a teacher trained on ground-truth labels and a student trained on fresh inputs labeled by that teacher. It reports scaling-law comparisons and theoretical conditions, but does not calculate Burns et al.'s PGR or compare against a strong model's true-label ceiling. Figure 1 checks whether deterministic equivalents track student errors; it does not compare student performance with the teacher, so those results are not rows here. Claims from cited papers are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study tests weak-to-strong training in a new setting: teacher and student are both random feature ridge regression models, and the student is trained only on teacher labels. It reports theory (Theorem 4, Corollaries 1–3) and simulations (Figure 2) comparing student and teacher test-error decay exponents. Its own results bear on whether the student beats its supervisor (V1), what drives the gain (V3), and conditions for it (V5). It is not an original source. It does not compute PGR.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in RFRR a student trained on teacher labels can attain a better test-error scaling law than the teacher, in both variance-dominated and bias-dominated regimes. Proper regularization and over-parameterization make this possible, unlike ridgeless linear regression. The student can reach the minimax rate even when the teacher's error does not decay. It cannot beat the scaling of an optimally tuned teacher. Their framework does not capture early stopping.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a two-stage RFRR procedure: a teacher is trained on ground-truth samples, then a student is trained on fresh inputs labeled by that teacher. Its main claims concern theoretical and simulated asymptotic excess-test-error scaling, not pretrained language-model fine-tuning or PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on teacher and student regularization, feature counts, student sample counts, source-capacity parameters, and whether the teacher is variance-dominated, bias-dominated, or optimally tuned. The theory requires zt > zs for improvement; in the bias-reduction regime it also requires r > 1/2 and student width greater than teacher width.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The paper does not report PGR or a true-label strong-model ceiling. Empirical scaling plots average 25 independent experiments and report one-standard-deviation confidence intervals, but numerical interval values are not stated. The experiments are RFRR simulations rather than pretrained AI models.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1's single-index and MNIST results are omitted because they validate student-error deterministic equivalents without comparing student performance with the teacher. The paper's detailed deterministic-equivalent approximation guarantees are not separate supervisor-versus-student outcomes.

untested.parts: Finite-sample PGR. Gains at constant level rather than in the exponent. Pretrained strong models with a true-label ceiling.
All: no confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants.
NLP, chess and reward-modelling tasks. Pretrained model size. Representation-based predictors.
All: no exploitation of checking limits, no distribution shift, no error-similarity analysis.
All: the MNIST plot only validates the deterministic equivalent; it does not compare student with teacher.

missing.what: Kernel limit and approximation limit. Gains then come only from variance reduction, only for sub-optimal teachers. In the variance-reduction case the student width must be smaller than the teacher width.
In the bias-reduction regime the scaling law can improve even when τt² = 0, i.e. when the teacher was trained on clean labels.

record.verdict_notes: The 'weak' teacher here is weak through mis-regularization or noise, not through capacity. In the variance-reduction case the student is narrower than the teacher, so results bear on V1 only loosely as a 'weak-to-strong' effect. All comparisons concern asymptotic exponents; no PGR or constant-level gains are reported. Tranche could arguably be T5 for V5, but T3 fits the main contribution.

versions.untested_parts: The paper compares excess-test-error scaling, not finite-sample PGR, and does not measure a strong pretrained model's ceiling on true labels.
No auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, or comparison of loss variants.

The study varies teacher/student sample counts, feature counts, regularization, and source-capacity parameters in RFRR. It does not test NLP, chess, reward modelling, pretrained-model size, or representations.
No test of exploiting a supervisor's checking limits, distribution shift, or gains shrinking when teacher and student errors are alike.
The theory concerns specified RFRR source-capacity and parameter-scaling assumptions; it does not establish a universal guarantee outside those assumptions.
No vision weak-to-strong experiment; the MNIST plot is used to check deterministic-equivalent predictions, not to compare student and teacher performance.

rows.subject: RFRR student
rows.size_stated: Feature and sample counts scale as powers of nt; zt and zs summarize effective teacher and student scaling.
rows.operation_detail: Derive a necessary condition for improvement in the student scaling law.
rows.value: Improvement is possible only if zt > zs; when zt ≤ zs, the teacher bias or variance induces student error terms at least of the same order.
rows.note: This is a necessary-condition result, not a claim that zt > zs alone guarantees improvement.
rows.check: Corollary 1 is a derived necessary condition: improvement only if zt > zs. That condition is fully established, so for V3 (what predicts the gain) and V5 (conditions) the state should be observed, not partial. Being necessary rather than sufficient is a matter of content, not a weaker effect.

source_check.notes: Theorem 4 establishes deterministic-equivalent rates; Section 4 requires an additional approximation-error condition to transfer them to actual risk and explicitly leaves broader guarantees open. These results concern RFRR scaling, not pretrained-model fine-tuning or measured PGR.

statements.correction: Figure 2: synthetic Gaussian model; 25 independent experiments; bands at one standard deviation. Figure 1: single-index synthetic data and MNIST; 10 independent experiments; bands at one standard deviation. MNIST validates deterministic-equivalent predictions, rather than demonstrating the claimed scaling-law improvement.
statements.problem: The cited scaling results and Figure 2 experiment count are correct, but the study also evaluates real MNIST data. The blanket descriptions of no real tasks and plots averaging 25 experiments omit Figure 1.

statements.correction: V3: supports dependence on teacher regime, model width and regularization. Figure 2(c): α=1.2, r=0.9; no scaling-law improvement. Optimized student and teacher exponents are equal. No conclusion about equality of their finite-sample errors follows from exponent equality alone.
statements.problem: The reported parameter values and exponent boundaries match the text. These dependencies support V3's predictive question; they do not establish a limitation of V3. Disappearance of exponent improvement also does not exclude constant-factor performance gains.

statements.correction: Training: ridge regression. Early stopping: not directly captured by the framework. Strict exponent improvement: conditional on Corollary 2 or Corollary 3 inequalities. zt>zs: necessary, not sufficient. Theorem 4 directly establishes rates for deterministic equivalents.
statements.problem: The necessary condition and conditional improvement regions are correct. The opening early-stopping description does not apply to this study, and suboptimal teacher tuning alone does not guarantee improvement for arbitrary student settings.
